normalized.governing_thought: Parcelbird should not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027 and should put the cash into scaling its software instead
executive_summary: Quick commerce is growing fast, but no operator has made it pay – US sales grew from $1.8B in 2022 to $5.1B in 2025, yet both incumbents lose money on every order (p. 4–6)

At the inputs Parcelbird's own customer sites achieve, every order loses money – A median-site order loses $6.17, and even the best observed inputs lose $1.76; The plan's profit needs every driver above the best site, a mix no site has reached (p. 8–11)

Customers stay less and cost more to win than the plan needs – 22% of pop-up customers still ordered in month three; 44% of residents said weekly; Even on plan, a customer who stays takes about 28 months to repay their acquisition cost (p. 13, 14)

The launch breaks the investors' runway floor even if everything goes to plan – Runway falls to about 6 months by month 18, half the 12-month floor; At median inputs, nine stores would lose about $18M a year (p. 16, 17)

Scaling the software for grocers who want their own fast delivery is the better use of cash – The pipeline could add $3.6M of ARR for about $1.2M of new cash to month 18, against $9.5M for the launch (p. 19–21)

slides.title: A growing market no one has made pay
Quick commerce is a real market, with US sales nearly tripling in three years to $5.1B in 2025

claims.claim: US sales nearly tripling in three years to $5.1B in 2025
evidence: US quick-commerce grocery sales (GMV), $B: 2022 1.8; 2023 2.6; 2024 3.6; 2025 5.1
2.8x growth in GMV from 2022 to 2025, the founders' main argument for entering now

claims.claim: 2023–25: growth of 38–44% every year, in line with the founders' claim of over 40% a year
evidence: Growth rates are year over year from Table 1 of the briefing pack

claims.claim: Scope: national sales only; the pack has no Midwest figure to test the claim that nobody owns the region
sales growth says nothing about whether anyone earns money on an order, which the next page tests

slides.title: Yet growth has not brought profit, and both incumbents lose money at EBITDA and on every order they deliver

claims.claim: Both lose a quarter or more of revenue at EBITDA
evidence: EBITDA margin 2025: Zipcart (national) -25.83%; QuickBasket (regional) -45.71%
Zipcart −$310M on $1,200M; QuickBasket −$96M on $210M

claims.claim: The smaller, regional operator loses more on each order
evidence: Contribution per order 2025: Zipcart -$1.9; QuickBasket -$3.4
the pack does not define the incumbents' contribution

claims.claim: a regional operator, the model Parcelbird Now would follow, is already retreating
evidence: QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025

slides.title: The founders' proof point is thin: Zipcart's densest city earns $0.40 an order, and only after a new $3.99 fee

claims.claim: The national leader loses money across its network
evidence: Zipcart lost $1.90 on the average order across its network in 2025
Its densest city is its most favorable market, not a typical one
Density alone had not made that city profitable

claims.claim: It got there by charging more and discounting less
evidence: Added a new service fee on every order, on top of delivery fees
Cut promotions to 1% of order value
Accepted the loss of volume that followed
$0.4 contribution per order in that city after the changes
$3.99 new service fee charged on every order
−14% change in order volume in that city afterwards

claims.claim: Parcelbird's plan expects five times that profit per order, with no service fee at all

slides.title: Unit economics at observed inputs
At the median of Parcelbird's own customer sites, every order loses $6.17, and riders are the largest cost

claims.claim: every order loses $6.17, and riders are the largest cost
evidence: $ per order: Gross margin on goods 9.18; Delivery fee 1.99; Picking and packing -3.1; Rider cost -7.3958; Payment and packaging -1.3; Promotions -2.04; Dark-store fixed cost -3.5008; Contribution per order -6.1666
Benchmark median of 14 Parcelbird software-customer sites, 2025

claims.claim: 43.2% of the loss arises before any store cost, so filling the stores cannot remove it on its own
Rider cost: $17.75 an hour spread over only 2.4 orders an hour
Dark-store fixed cost: $1.15M a year per store spread over 900 orders a day
Promotions: 6% of a $34 basket handed back, more than the whole delivery fee collected

slides.title: Even the best inputs seen at any customer site lose $1.76 an order; only the founders' plan makes money

claims.claim: Every case Parcelbird has observed loses money; the plan is the outlier
evidence: Contribution per order: Pop-up test, Columbus -12.5725; Benchmark median -6.1666; Best observed (composite) -1.7572; Founders' plan 2.0182

claims.claim: Pop-up test: a $31 basket, promotions at 12% and 280 orders a day put a heavy store cost on each order
evidence: The pop-up uses its own annualized fixed cost of $650,000 for a temporary site

claims.claim: Benchmark median: the typical site Parcelbird's software runs, the fair base case for mid-size Midwest cities
Best observed: the best basket and best density came from different sites; no single site reached both
Founders' plan: positive only on inputs beyond the best observed

slides.title: The plan needs a bigger basket, faster riders, fuller stores and smaller promotions than any site has reached

claims.claim: The plan needs a bigger basket, faster riders, fuller stores and smaller promotions than any site has reached
evidence: Benchmark median: $34 basket; 2.4 orders per rider-hour; 900 orders per store a day; 6% promotions
Pop-up test, Columbus: $31; 2.1; 280; 12% — Below the benchmark range on orders a day, twice the median's promotions
Best observed (composite): $42; 3; 1,400; 6% — Best basket and best density came from different sites
Founders' plan: $45; 3.5; 1,800; 2% — Beyond anything observed / Above the top of the benchmark range on riders and store volume, with 6.4 times the pop-up's daily orders
Benchmark range across the 14 sites: 1.9–3.0 orders per rider-hour and 400–1,400 orders per store a day

slides.title: At median costs, an order would break even only with a basket of about $63, far above any site observed

claims.claim: At median costs, an order would break even only with a basket of about $63
evidence: $13.3 cost per order that does not grow with the basket: picking, riders, payment, packaging and store, less the delivery fee
÷ 21% kept from each basket dollar: 27% gross margin on goods less 6% in promotions
= $63.4 basket value at which a median-cost order breaks even
For comparison, the median basket is $34, the best observed $42 and the pop-up's $31

claims.claim: The break-even holds only if median costs stay flat as baskets grow
evidence: Rider, picking, payment and store costs stay at the benchmark median of the 14 customer sites
Gross margin on goods stays at 27% and promotions at 6% of the basket

claims.claim: Larger baskets would likely cost more to pick, so the true break-even basket is higher

slides.title: Customer evidence
Real use falls short of stated intent: fewer customers stay, and those who stay order less than once a week

claims.claim: Half as many kept ordering as said they would use it weekly
evidence: Survey (n = 1,500): would use it at least weekly 44%; Pop-up: still ordering in month three 22%
The survey covers Columbus residents aged 25–39, the pop-up all its customers: the shares show the direction, not an exact gap

claims.claim: Those who stayed ordered less than once a week
evidence: 0.7 orders a week from each customer still ordering in month three
Equal to 3.1 orders a month
Orders a week = 3.1 a month × 12 ÷ 52

claims.claim: The plan's store volumes need frequent repeat use
The pop-up's 18% weekly order growth came with promotions at 12% of the basket, twice the median site's 6%

slides.title: Even on the plan's own economics, a customer who stays would take about 28 months to repay their acquisition cost

claims.claim: a customer who stays would take about 28 months to repay their acquisition cost
evidence: $38 to win one customer at the pop-up, through paid social and first-order credits
÷ 22% of customers still ordering in month three
÷ $6.3 contribution a month from each customer who stays: 3.1 orders × $2.02 in the founders' plan
= 27.6 months to repay the cost of each customer who stays

claims.claim: The payback assumes the pop-up's customer data holds at scale
evidence: Acquisition cost stays at the pop-up's $38 per customer and month-three retention at 22%
Customers who stay keep ordering 3.1 times a month
Orders from customers who leave before month three are not counted

claims.claim: at the benchmark median every order loses money and the cost is never repaid

slides.title: Cash and runway
On the founders' own plan, the launch would leave about 6 months of runway by mid-2028, half the investors' floor

claims.claim: the launch would leave about 6 months of runway by mid-2028, half the investors' floor
evidence: Cash, $M: Cash today 12; Nine dark stores (capex) 5.4; Launch marketing and operating losses 4.1; Cash at month 18 2.5
6.3 months of runway left at month 18 at today's burn, against the 12 months the investors require

claims.claim: Operating losses: sized on the plan's inputs; larger at observed inputs
If the $9.5M excludes today's $0.4M monthly burn: cash runs out before month 18
evidence: If it is the launch only, month-18 cash = $12.0M − $9.5M − 18 × $0.4M = −$4.7M

claims.claim: The launch fails the investors' runway condition before any execution risk

slides.title: At median inputs, nine stores would lose about $18M a year, more than all the cash in the bank

claims.claim: nine stores would lose about $18M a year, more than all the cash in the bank
evidence: 9 dark stores in the founders' plan
× 328,500 orders a year per store at the median of 900 a day, every day of the year
× −$6.2 contribution per order at benchmark median inputs, after store costs
= −$18.2M a year for the network, against $12.0M of cash in the bank

claims.claim: The loss recurs every year, and only the plan's own inputs turn it around
evidence: With the best observed inputs combined, the network would still lose about $8.1M a year; only the founders' plan earns money, about $11.9M

claims.claim: minimum pay rules weighed in two of the three cities would deepen the loss
evidence: Rider pay stays at $17.75 an hour

slides.title: The better path: scale the software
Selling to the grocers already in the pipeline could add $3.6M of ARR for about $0.8M a year of new hires

claims.claim: $3.6M of new ARR if all 37 pipeline grocers sign
evidence: 87% of today's ARR of $4.1M
Average contract of $96,000 a year
Builds on ARR already growing 60% a year
the pack does not give win rates, so the full pipeline is an upper bound

claims.claim: $864K of ARR from the 9 late-stage grocers alone
evidence: The near-term part of the pipeline
Several of these grocers want fast delivery from their own stores, which the software runs
About $700K of gross profit a year at the 81% software margin
That covers about 87% of a year of the new hires

claims.claim: $0.8M a year for 2 more engineers and 2 sales hires
evidence: About $67K a month on top of today's $0.4M burn
No stores, riders or inventory to fund
Runway today stays at about 26 months with the hires
Without a launch, today's burn leaves exactly 12 months of runway at month 18

claims.claim: New contracts therefore have to pay for the hires

slides.title: At about $1.2M to mid-2028, against $9.5M for the launch, scaling the software is the better use of cash

claims.claim: scaling the software is the better use of cash
evidence: Launch Parcelbird Now, nine stores: $9.5M new cash to month 18 — No: loses money at every observed input and breaks the runway floor
Launch a smaller test first: Not in the plan — No: the autumn pop-up already tested one site and lost money on every order
Scale the software: $1.2M — Recommended / Serves the grocers who want fast delivery from their own stores instead of competing with them
Software: two engineers and two sales hires for 18 months, before any new revenue

slides.title: The board could reopen the operator question only once four conditions hold, and none holds today

claims.claim: A customer site makes money per order after store costs — not met
evidence: −$1.8 per order with the best observed inputs

claims.claim: Customers stay long enough to repay their acquisition cost — not met
evidence: 22% of pop-up customers still ordering in month three

claims.claim: Rider pay rules are settled in the launch cities — not met
evidence: 2 of three cities weighing minimum rider pay

claims.claim: Outside funding covers the launch instead of the runway — not met
evidence: 6.3 months of runway at month 18 on the plan
The lead investor calls a new funding round for a delivery operator "unlikely in this market"

claims.claim: Until then, Parcelbird should sell grocers the software to run their own fast delivery, not compete with them

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Parcelbird should not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027 and should put the cash into scaling its software instead; until four conditions hold, Parcelbird should sell grocers the software to run their own fast delivery, not compete with them.

alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: $9.5M new cash to month 18; "No: loses money at every observed input and breaks the runway floor"
Rejected: new cash "Not in the plan"; "No: the autumn pop-up already tested one site and lost money on every order"
Recommended: $1.2M new cash to month 18; "Serves the grocers who want fast delivery from their own stores instead of competing with them"

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Scope: national sales only; the pack has no Midwest figure to test the claim that nobody owns the region
The pack does not define the incumbents' contribution
Contribution after dark-store fixed cost; before head-office costs, capex and customer acquisition
The pop-up uses its own annualized fixed cost of $650,000 for a temporary site
The break-even holds only if median costs stay flat as baskets grow; larger baskets would likely cost more to pick, so the true break-even basket is higher
The survey covers Columbus residents aged 25–39, the pop-up all its customers: the shares show the direction, not an exact gap

The payback assumes the pop-up's customer data holds at scale: acquisition cost $38, month-three retention 22%, 3.1 orders a month, $2.02 contribution; orders from customers who leave before month three are not counted
Operating losses sized on the plan's inputs; larger at observed inputs
Generous reading: the $9.5M is the full cash need. If it is the launch only, month-18 cash = −$4.7M and cash runs out before month 18
Each of the nine stores runs all year at the median of 900 orders a day; rider pay stays at $17.75 an hour; minimum pay rules weighed in two of the three cities would deepen the loss
The pack does not give win rates, so the full pipeline is an upper bound
Software cost: two engineers and two sales hires for 18 months, before any new revenue; new contracts have to pay for the hires
The lead investor calls a new funding round for a delivery operator "unlikely in this market"
next_steps: Decline the Parcelbird Now launch and record the four conditions for reopening it — Board — January 2027
Hire the two engineers and two sales staff to scale the software — CEO — Q1 2027
Close the late-stage grocers, leading with fast delivery from their own stores — Head of sales — H1 2027
Set a burn plan that keeps 12 months of runway beyond mid-2028 — CFO — Q1 2027
Track customer sites and rider pay rules against the four conditions — Founders — Quarterly from Q2 2027
normalized.extraction_notes: The deck came as plain text with no images. The rating circles (Harvey balls) in the slide 20 table were not in the text, so the per-criterion ratings for the three options could not be extracted. The slide 10 table also uses shading to rank rows within each column; that shading was not captured, but the numbers were. The slide 16 chart is a waterfall built as a stacked chart, so its 'base' series is invisible spacing and only the 'Cash' values were recorded. The executive-summary page references (p. 4–6 and so on) were kept inline. The status markers 'not met' on the slide 21 claims were added from the slide title 'none holds today'.
